books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

primary_sources: Grover Cleveland, veto message on the Texas Seed Bill, February 16, 1887
Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889
William Jennings Bryan, “Cross of Gold” speech, July 9, 1896

prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the role of the federal government in the American economy changed in the period 1865–1898.

documents.title: Chief Justice Waite on Property and the Public
documents.source: Munn v. Illinois, 94 U.S. 113 (1877), majority opinion of Chief Justice Morrison Waite. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The Chief Justice writing for a 7-2 majority, upholding a state law that set maximum charges for grain storage.
documents.text: “Property does become clothed with a public interest when used in a manner to make it of public consequence, and affect the community at large. When, therefore, one devotes his property to a use in which the public has an interest, he, in effect, grants to the public an interest in that use, and must submit to be controlled by the public for the common good, to the extent of the interest he has thus created.”

documents.title: Cleveland Vetoes Seed Aid
documents.source: President Grover Cleveland, veto message on the Texas Seed Bill, February 16, 1887. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Democratic president writing to Congress to explain why he refused $10,000 in seed aid for drought-stricken Texas farmers.
documents.text: “I can find no warrant for such an appropriation in the Constitution, and I do not believe that the power and duty of the General Government ought to be extended to the relief of individual suffering which is in no manner properly related to the public service or benefit. A prevalent tendency to disregard the limited mission of this power and duty should, I think, be steadfastly resisted, to the end that the lesson should be constantly enforced that, though the people support the Government, the Government should not support the people.”

documents.title: The Interstate Commerce Act on Railroad Charges
documents.source: Interstate Commerce Act, Section 1, February 4, 1887. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A federal law written after the Supreme Court barred the states from regulating interstate railroad rates.
documents.text: “All charges made for any service rendered or to be rendered in the transportation of passengers or property as aforesaid, or in connection therewith, or for the receiving, delivering, storage, or handling of such property, shall be reasonable and just; and every unjust and unreasonable charge for such service is prohibited and declared to be unlawful.”

documents.title: Carnegie on the Administration of Wealth
documents.source: Andrew Carnegie, “Wealth,” North American Review, June 1889. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A steel maker writing for a magazine read by the educated middle class, arguing that the rich should give while they lived.
documents.text:
“The problem of our age is the proper administration of wealth, so that the ties of brotherhood may still bind together the rich and poor in harmonious relationship.”

“There are but three modes in which surplus wealth can be disposed of. It can be left to the families of the decedents; or it can be bequeathed for public purposes; or, finally, it can be administered during their lives by its possessors.”

documents.title: The Sherman Antitrust Act on Restraint of Trade
documents.source: Sherman Antitrust Act, Section 1, July 2, 1890. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The first federal antitrust law, written to keep monopolistic practices in check.
documents.text: “Every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations, is hereby declared to be illegal.”

documents.title: The Omaha Platform on the Railroads
documents.source: People's Party, Omaha Platform, July 4, 1892, Platform. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A new third party’s founding statement, written to indict the old parties and rally farmers and workers.
documents.text: “Third.—We believe that the time has come when the railroad corporations will either own the people or the people must own the railroads, and should the government enter upon the work of owning and managing all railroads, we should favor an amendment to the Constitution by which all persons engaged in the government service shall be placed under a civil-service regulation of the most rigid character, so as to prevent the increase of the power of the national administration by the use of such additional government employes.”

documents.title: Bryan on the Cross of Gold
documents.source: William Jennings Bryan, “Cross of Gold” speech, Democratic National Convention, Chicago, July 9, 1896. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A former Nebraska congressman addressing his party’s convention, arguing that the gold standard crushed farmers and workers.
documents.text: “You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns, you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.”

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the federal government’s role in the economy changed between 1865 and 1898, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent of change does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as industrialization building giant corporations and crowded cities, or the older American suspicion of government power.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing specific and relevant evidence from at least three documents to support an argument.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than three documents, or quoting documents without describing what they show, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support an argument, with the evidence accurately described and tied to the claim.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or listing documents without connecting them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific and relevant example beyond the documents, such as the Wabash decision of 1886, the E. C. Knight decision of 1895, Coxey’s Army of 1894, or the election of 1896.
rubric.notEarned: A general statement with no specific example beyond the documents does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining the relevance of a document’s author, purpose, audience, or historical situation to the argument, for at least two documents.
rubric.notEarned: Identifying an author without explaining why it matters, or sourcing only one document, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for demonstrating a complex understanding, such as qualifying the extent of change, showing that the same government both expanded regulation and guarded property, or explaining why one reform succeeded while another stalled.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Between 1865 and 1898 the federal government’s role in the economy changed a great deal in what Americans asked of it, moving from a hands-off state toward one expected to regulate railroads and trusts, relieve suffering, and manage the money supply, though the change stayed partial because presidents, courts, and the limits of the new laws blocked much of it.
Context: Industrialization built giant corporations and crowded cities, while farmers faced falling prices and railroad rates they could not control, and the older American suspicion of strong government still shaped how presidents and judges answered new demands.
Evidence: Documents 1 and 3 show regulation taking hold, as Munn let the public control property clothed with a public interest and the Interstate Commerce Act required railroad charges to be reasonable and just. Documents 5 and 6 show the demand widening, as the Sherman Act outlawed restraints of trade and the Populists called for the people to own the railroads.
Evidence continued: Documents 2 and 4 show the other side, as Cleveland vetoed seed aid for Texas farmers and Carnegie argued that the rich themselves, not the government, should administer wealth. Document 7 shows the money question reaching its peak, as Bryan charged that the gold standard crucified mankind.
Beyond the documents: The Wabash decision of 1886 barred the states from regulating interstate rates, which forced Congress to act, and the E. C. Knight decision of 1895 then narrowed the Sherman Act to trade rather than manufacturing. Coxey’s Army marched on Washington in 1894 asking for federal jobs, and McKinley’s victory in 1896 settled the money question for gold.
Sourcing: Cleveland writes as a president defending a veto, so his claim about the Constitution serves his policy, while the Omaha Platform is a new party’s own case for itself, so its charges are a program, not a neutral report. Carnegie writes as a rich man defending his own class to magazine readers.
Complexity: Government grew in law and in demands, yet the same government still guarded property, the courts narrowed the Sherman Act in E. C. Knight, and the farmers and workers who asked for the most gained the least from the laws that passed.
